46432: Spinoza and the rise of historical criticism
46433: Baruch Spinoza's *Theological-Political Treatise* (1670) argues that the Bible must be studied like nature, from its own history and language alone, without assuming it is divine. Questions about who wrote what and when become central in the European Enlightenment.
46435: Friedrich Schleiermacher's lectures on hermeneutics (given between 1805 and 1833, published after his death in 1838) treat understanding any text as an art: grasping both its language and the mind of its author. Hermeneutics becomes a general theory of understanding, not only rules for the Bible.
46437: Julius Wellhausen's history of Israel (1878, later titled *Prolegomena to the History of Israel*) popularises the theory that the Pentateuch was combined from four sources (J, E, D, P). It dominated critical scholarship for a century and is now heavily revised or contested.
46439: Karl Barth's commentary on Romans (1919, rewritten 1922) protests that historical study had stopped hearing Scripture as God's living word. He calls for interpretation that lets the text speak as divine address, a key spark for later theological interpretation.
46441: Evangelical scholars meeting in Chicago issue the *Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy* (1978), followed by the *Chicago Statement on Biblical Hermeneutics* (1982). The second affirms the grammatical-historical method, attention to genre, and the single meaning of a text with many applications.
46443: Brevard Childs' *Introduction to the Old Testament as Scripture* (1979) argues that the final shape of the biblical books, as received by synagogue and church, is the proper focus of interpretation for the community of faith.
46444: Robert Alter's *The Art of Biblical Narrative* (1981) shows the subtle skill of Hebrew storytelling: repetition, dialogue, type-scenes and silence. Narrative criticism of the Gospels grows alongside it in the 1980s.
46446: The *Dictionary for Theological Interpretation of the Bible* (edited by Kevin Vanhoozer, 2005) and the *Journal of Theological Interpretation* (from 2007) mark a movement to read the Bible as Scripture for the church, drawing on creeds and pre-modern interpreters as well as modern study.
46448: The *Africa Bible Commentary* (2006), written by African scholars, and later the *South Asia Bible Commentary* (2015), show how readers in collectivist, honour-based and multi-faith cultures often see things Western readers miss. Writers such as Randolph Richards and Brandon O'Brien make the same point for Western readers.
46449: Jewish-context readings of the New Testament
46450: *The Jewish Annotated New Testament* (edited by Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Zvi Brettler, 2011) gathers Jewish scholars to explain the New Testament's Jewish setting. Christian writers such as Marvin Wilson, Lois Tverberg and Kenneth Bailey help believers read Jesus as a Jewish teacher within Israel's covenant life.
46452: Each card explains a kind of biblical writing or a key term in interpretation. Filter by colour to see where each idea comes from: the genres of the Old Testament (and Jewish reading terms) are marked as ancient Jewish; the New Testament genres and early Christian terms as apostles and early church; later terms by the era that named them.
46454: Stories that show God at work in history.
46455: About 40 percent of the Old Testament is narrative. Biblical stories are told briefly and artfully; the narrator often reports without commenting, so we must not assume that what a person did is what God approved. The main character of every biblical story is God.
46459: Covenant instruction for a rescued people.
46460: Torah means teaching or instruction. The laws were given after the exodus, as the terms of a relationship, not a ladder to earn it. They include worship, justice, family and daily life. Christians debate how each law applies after Christ.
46463: Prayers and songs built on parallel lines and images.
46464: Hebrew poetry rhymes ideas more than sounds. Psalms include praise, lament, thanksgiving, royal and wisdom psalms. They teach us how to speak to God in every season, including anger and grief.
46468: Reflection on how to live well in God's world.
46469: Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs explore life's order and its puzzles. Job and Ecclesiastes must be read as whole arguments, because some speeches are later corrected.
46471: Short sayings about what usually happens, not promises.
46472: A proverb is a general truth stated memorably. 'Train up a child' describes how life usually goes, not a guarantee for every family. Paired proverbs that seem to clash (answer a fool, do not answer a fool) teach wise judgement.
46473: Covenant preaching: warning, call to return, and hope.
46474: Prophets were God's messengers enforcing the covenant. Most of their words address their own time. Fee and Stuart estimate that less than 2 percent of Old Testament prophecy is messianic, less than 5 percent describes the new-covenant age, and less than 1 percent concerns events still future to us. Many warnings are conditional on repentance.
46477: Symbolic visions revealing who rules history.
46478: Apocalyptic writing grew in Jewish circles (Daniel, 1 Enoch) and is continued in Revelation. Its beasts, numbers and colours are a picture language drawn from the Old Testament. It comforts persecuted believers that God and the Lamb will win.
46480: Ancient biographies of Jesus with a message.
46481: The four Gospels resemble Greco-Roman lives (bioi) but proclaim good news. Each writer selects and arranges material for his audience, so reading 'horizontally' (comparing parallels) and 'vertically' (following one Gospel's story) both help.
46483: Short, surprising stories that call for a response.
46484: Parables were a familiar Jewish teaching form (the rabbis told them too). They usually make one or a few main points tied to their audience. Jesus sometimes explained details symbolically, but readers should be cautious about turning every detail into a code.
46489: New Testament letters follow ancient letter forms (greeting, thanksgiving, body, closing). They were read aloud to gathered churches. We hear one side of a conversation, so we reconstruct the situation carefully and humbly.
46492: Reading meaning out of the text, not into it.
46493: Exegesis (Greek: 'leading out') draws out what the text says. Eisegesis ('leading in') reads our own ideas into it. All readers drift toward eisegesis; method, community and the Spirit help us correct it.
46495: The words, book, history and culture around a passage.
46496: Literary context is the surrounding text; historical-cultural context is the world behind it; canonical context is the whole Bible. A verse without context becomes a pretext for whatever we want it to say.
46500: What the author meant to communicate.
46501: E. D. Hirsch argued that the author's intended meaning is the only stable norm for interpretation. Kevin Vanhoozer reframed it as the author's 'communicative act'. Critics note that we know authors only through their texts and that God may mean more than the human writer saw.
46506: A 'fuller sense' intended by God beyond the human author's awareness.
46507: The Latin phrase means 'fuller sense'. Catholic scholars in the twentieth century (notably Raymond Brown) developed it to explain how texts like Isaiah 7:14 can mean more in Christ. Some evangelicals accept it in a limited form; others prefer to speak of typology or canonical meaning.
46511: Real history as patterns that God fulfils later.
46512: A type (Greek typos, 'pattern' or 'imprint') is a real person, event or institution that foreshadows a later, greater fulfilment. The New Testament sees types in Adam, the flood, the Passover lamb, the wilderness and the temple.
46516: Finding a second, symbolic meaning in a text's details.
46517: Some texts are allegories by design (Ezekiel's eagles, some parables). Allegorical interpretation goes further, reading spiritual meanings into ordinary stories. Paul does it once (Gal 4:24). Used carefully under the rule of faith it fed devotion; used freely it lets readers make texts say anything.
46520: A mirror pattern: A-B-B'-A', often with the key point at the centre.
46521: Named after the Greek letter chi (X), a chiasm repeats ideas in reverse order. It helped hearers remember and highlighted the centre. Small examples are clear; large ones proposed for whole books are sometimes over-ingenious.
46524: Bookends: the same words at the start and end of a section.
46525: An inclusio marks the boundaries of a unit and its theme. Psalm 8 begins and ends with the same praise. Matthew frames Jesus' teaching and healing in chapters 5 to 9 with almost identical summaries.
46527: Lines that echo, contrast or build on each other.
46528: Robert Lowth (1753) described Hebrew parallelism as synonymous, antithetic and synthetic. Recent scholars (James Kugel, Robert Alter) show the second line usually sharpens or intensifies the first: 'A, and what's more, B'.
46531: Deliberate exaggeration to make a point.
46532: Jesus uses Jewish teaching hyperbole: tear out your eye, a camel through a needle's eye, swallowing a camel. Reading it as literal instruction misses its force; ignoring it misses its seriousness.
46536: Expressions whose meaning is not the sum of their words.
46537: 'Hate your father' in Luke 14:26 is a Semitic idiom for 'love less' (compare Gen 29:30-31, where Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah and Leah is called 'hated'). A 'good eye' or 'evil eye' referred to generosity or stinginess.
46539: A binding, loyal relationship sealed by promise.
46540: Covenant (Hebrew berit) is the Bible's main way of describing God's relationship with people. The covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel, David and the new covenant form the backbone of the story. Ancient treaties help explain their shape.
46545: God's kingdom has begun in Jesus but is not yet complete.
46546: Jesus announced the kingdom as present, yet taught his followers to pray for it to come. This tension shapes how we read promises: some are fulfilled now in part and will be fulfilled fully later. Geerhardus Vos, Oscar Cullmann and George Eldon Ladd developed the idea.
46549: God revealed himself step by step through history.
46550: God spoke 'in many ways' before speaking fully in his Son. Later revelation does not contradict earlier revelation but completes it. This explains why some practices (sacrifices, food laws) change after Christ.
46551: Rule of faith / analogy of faith
46552: Read each passage in harmony with the whole faith.
46553: The early 'rule of faith' (Irenaeus, Tertullian) summarised the apostolic gospel as a guide for reading. The Reformers' 'analogy of faith' means Scripture interprets Scripture: unclear passages are read in light of clear ones.
46555: The Spirit helps believers understand and receive Scripture.
46556: Inspiration is the Spirit's work in giving Scripture; illumination is his work in readers. Calvin spoke of the inner witness of the Spirit that convinces us Scripture is God's word. Illumination does not reveal new meanings but helps us grasp and embrace the meaning.
46560: Jewish 'searching' of Scripture to draw out teaching.
46561: Midrash (from darash, 'to seek') links texts, explores gaps and applies Scripture to life, through law (halakhah) and story (aggadah). The Hebrew word appears in Chronicles for written records or commentaries. New Testament writers sometimes argue in midrashic ways.
46565: 'This is that': prophecy applied to the present community.
46566: Pesher means 'interpretation'. The Qumran scrolls read prophetic verses line by line as being fulfilled in their own day. Peter's 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel' at Pentecost has a similar shape, centred on Jesus.
46573: In the human author's intended meaning, expressed in words, genre and setting
46574: What did the author mean to the first readers?
46575: Guards against reading our ideas into the text; gives shared, checkable results
46576: Can stop at 'then' and never reach Christ, the church or today; can underplay the divine author
46577: Most evangelical scholars and seminaries; the Chicago Statement on Hermeneutics
46579: In spiritual realities behind the literal details
46580: What deeper truth about Christ, the soul or heaven does this picture?
46581: Reads all Scripture as nourishing faith and love; takes the divine author seriously
46582: Meaning becomes arbitrary and controlled by the reader's ideas
46583: Philo, Origen, many church fathers and medieval preachers; parts of Orthodox and Catholic devotion
46585: In patterns God built into real history, fulfilled later
46586: How does this person or event foreshadow what God does in Christ?
46587: Follows the New Testament's own practice; keeps history real
46588: Seeing types everywhere without textual warrant
46589: The apostles, the church fathers, Reformed and Catholic interpreters alike
46590: In the literal sense plus allegorical, moral and anagogical senses
46591: What happened, what should I believe, do and hope?
46592: Holds study and devotion together; every text speaks to faith, life and hope
46593: Spiritual senses can drift far from the letter
46594: Medieval Western church; renewed interest among Catholic and theological interpreters
46596: In the text's place in the unfolding history of salvation
46597: What stage of God's plan is this, and how does it lead to Christ?
46598: Shows the Bible's unity and avoids moralising stories
46599: Can flatten each passage into 'the same sermon'; may neglect ethics
46600: Reformed biblical theology: Vos, Clowney, Goldsworthy, Greidanus
46601: In the text's original historical setting and the history of its composition
46602: How did this text arise, and what did it mean in its time?
46603: Rich knowledge of languages, history and how texts developed
46604: Naturalistic assumptions can exclude God's action; results can be speculative
46605: University biblical studies worldwide; used critically by many believing scholars
46607: In the final form of the text within the whole canon of the community
46608: How does this book function as Scripture alongside the others?
46609: Respects the Bible as received by synagogue and church; reunites study and faith
46610: Can bypass historical questions; which canon (Jewish, Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox)?
46611: Brevard Childs, Christopher Seitz, many theological interpreters
46613: In the story world: plot, character, point of view
46614: How does this story work and what does it invite us to see?
46615: Takes biblical artistry seriously; resists moralising fragments
46616: Can treat history as merely story; may lose the 'did it happen' question
46617: Robert Alter, Meir Sternberg, R. Alan Culpepper, many preachers
46618: In the encounter between the text and its readers or reading communities
46619: What does this text do to readers, and how do communities read it?
46620: Exposes hidden assumptions; values voices often unheard
46621: In strong forms the text can no longer correct the reader
46622: Stanley Fish, Wolfgang Iser; adapted by liberation, feminist and some Majority-World readers
46623: In God's communicative action through the text to the church
46624: What is God saying to his people through this text, read with the creeds?
46625: Restores Scripture as Scripture; learns from pre-modern readers
46626: Doctrine may override what the text actually says; definitions vary
46627: Kevin Vanhoozer, Daniel Treier, Stephen Fowl, Brazos commentary writers
46629: In the Spirit's present voice through the text, within the community
46630: How does the Spirit who inspired this text speak and act through it now?
46631: Expects transformation and experience of God; reads Acts as a living pattern
46632: Subjective impressions can override the text without careful testing
46633: Kenneth Archer, Amos Yong, Craig Keener, global Pentecostal churches
46635: In the covenant relationship and Jewish world of the first hearers
46636: How would Israel or Jesus' Jewish hearers have understood this?
46637: Recovers idioms, methods and the relational heart of Torah and gospel; counters anti-Jewish readings
46638: Can over-claim from later rabbinic sources or romanticise 'Hebrew thought'
46639: Marvin Wilson, Lois Tverberg, Kenneth Bailey, Amy-Jill Levine, N. T. Wright (in his own way)
46641: Interpreters differ on where the meaning of a text is anchored. At one end, meaning is fixed by the author in the original setting. At the other, meaning is made by readers and communities today. Almost everyone sits somewhere between, and most traditions hold several factors together. These placements are approximate and meant to start conversation, not to label anyone.
46645: A text means what its author willed it to mean; this meaning is fixed and determinate. Its significance for later readers can change, but its meaning cannot. This protects the text from being bent by readers.
46646: E. D. Hirsch (*Validity in Interpretation*, 1967); Walter Kaiser
46648: Meaning is found by reconstructing what the text meant in its historical setting and how it came to be. What it means for faith today is a separate question for theologians.
46649: Classic historical-critical scholarship (Krister Stendahl's 'what it meant' versus 'what it means')
46651: A text has one meaning, the author's, but many applications. The divine author stands behind the human author and the whole canon helps clarify the meaning.
46652: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart; the Chicago Statement on Biblical Hermeneutics (1982)
46654: Meaning is what the author does with words (promising, warning, comforting). Readers are called not only to grasp it but to perform it faithfully, like actors with a script. The author remains the anchor, but understanding is active.
46655: Kevin Vanhoozer (*Is There a Meaning in This Text?*, 1998); Anthony Thiselton
46657: Interpreters must seek what the human authors intended, using genre and history, and also read Scripture as a whole, within the living Tradition of the church, with the magisterium (teaching office) serving the word of God.
46658: Catholic Church (*Dei Verbum* 12, 1965; Pontifical Biblical Commission, 1993)
46659: Final form for the believing community
46660: Meaning is found in the final shape of the text as the community of faith received it as Scripture, not mainly in reconstructed earlier stages or in the individual reader.
46661: Brevard Childs and the canonical approach
46662: Scripture within the mind of the Fathers
46663: Scripture lives within the Church. Its meaning is received through the worship, the councils and the 'mind of the Fathers', where the historical sense opens into a spiritual vision (theoria) of Christ.
46664: Eastern Orthodox tradition (Georges Florovsky, John Breck)
46665: The world in front of the text
46666: Once written, a text gains a life beyond its author. Its meaning is the 'world' it opens up in front of readers, which they can inhabit. Careful explanation and personal understanding go together.
46669: Meaning emerges in the conversation between Scripture, the Spirit's present work and the discerning community. The Spirit who inspired the text speaks through it today, tested by Scripture and the church.
46670: Pentecostal hermeneutics (Kenneth Archer, Amos Yong); Craig Keener holds a more author-anchored version
46672: Understanding happens when the 'horizon' of the text meets the horizon of the reader, shaped by history and tradition. No one reads from nowhere, and every understanding is an event.
46675: Readers in situations of poverty, oppression or minority status see what comfortable readers miss. The social location of readers rightly shapes which meanings come to light.
46676: Liberation and contextual readings (Gustavo Gutierrez, R. S. Sugirtharajah)
46678: There is no meaning 'in' the text independent of readers. Communities of interpretation, with shared assumptions, determine what readers see.
46679: Stanley Fish (*Is There a Text in This Class?*, 1980)
46680: A promise of plans to prosper you?
46681: Is this God's personal promise that my career and life plans will succeed?
46683: God says he knows the plans he has for 'you' (in Hebrew, a plural 'you all'), plans for peace (shalom) and not evil, to give a future and a hope.
46685: This is part of a letter Jeremiah sent to the exiles in Babylon (29:1). Just before, God says they will stay 70 years (29:10), so they should build houses, marry and seek the welfare of Babylon (29:4-7).
46686: Many hearers would die in exile before the 70 years ended. False prophets were promising a quick return (29:8-9). The promise is for the people as a whole, after a long wait.
46688: God had not abandoned his covenant people. Judgement was real and long, but his purpose for Israel was restoration, and they should seek him wholeheartedly (29:12-14).
46690: The return from exile and the greater restoration the prophets promised point forward to the new covenant (Jer 31:31-34), fulfilled in Christ, who gathers a people and gives them a living hope.
46692: God's purposes for his people are good and faithful even in long, painful seasons. Today this encourages believers together to trust God, settle and seek the good of the place they are in, without treating the verse as a guarantee of personal success.
46693: The verse is a precious promise of God's faithfulness to his people, but it was spoken to a community in exile, with a long wait. Read in context, it is deeper than a career promise: it teaches patient hope and faithful living where God has placed us.
46695: Does this verse mean Christ will give me strength to win any contest or achieve any goal?
46696: Paul says he can do 'all things' through the one who strengthens him.
46697: The previous verses (4:10-12) are about money and circumstances: Paul has learned to be content when well fed and when hungry, in plenty and in need. 'All things' means 'all these circumstances'.
46698: Paul writes from prison, thanking the Philippians for a gift. In the Greco-Roman world, gifts created obligations; Paul gratefully receives the gift while making clear his security is in Christ, not in patrons.
46699: Christ gives Paul the strength to be content and faithful in any situation, including poverty and prison.
46700: Believers can face both success and loss with contentment through Christ's strength. An athlete can certainly apply this, but to lose well as much as to win.
46701: The verse is about contentment in every situation, not about achieving every goal. That is a stronger promise: Christ is enough in hunger as well as in plenty.
46702: Where two or three are gathered
46703: Is this verse mainly about small prayer meetings, assuring us Jesus is present when few attend?
46704: Matthew 18:15-20 is about restoring a brother or sister who sins: go privately, then with one or two others, then to the church. 'Two or three' echoes the rule of two or three witnesses (Deut 19:15).
46706: A saying later recorded in the Mishnah (Avot 3) teaches that when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, God's presence (the Shekhinah) rests with them. Jesus makes a similar but bolder claim: he himself is present.
46707: When the community seeks to discern and decide on discipline in Jesus' name, he is present with them, backing their faithful judgement.
